--- title: "[Graph.shortest_path()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find shortest path between two nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L40707-L40863){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.shortest_path( source, target, attr_name=None, return_list=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Shortest path (fewest hops)](/assets/graphs/shortest-path.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same directed weighted graph with three routes from A to F. shortest_path runs a breadth-first search, so it ignores the weights and returns the two-hop path A, D, F in the accent color, with filled badges giving each node's position 0, 1, 2." width="100%"} Finds a single shortest route from `source=` to `target=`. The meaning of "shortest" depends on how the graph was created: - for an unweighted graph (the default, `Graph(weighted=False)`), a breadth-first search (BFS) finds the path with the fewest hops, and any edge weights are ignored - for a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`), Dijkstra's algorithm finds the path with the lowest total edge weight; edges without a weight count as `1.0` In directed graphs, the path follows edge directions. If several paths are equally short, one of them is returned. Can return the path as a list, or store the position of each node along the path as a node attribute for visualization. Shortest paths are a basic building block for routing and navigation, tracing how two entities are connected (for example, the chain of contacts between two people), and highlighting a route in a plot. Dijkstra's algorithm assumes non-negative weights; if your graph has negative weights, use `bellman_ford_shortest_path()` instead. For heuristic or anytime search, see `ada_star_search()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node where the path starts, given as an integer node ID or a string label. An unknown label raises a `ValueError`; an integer ID that is not in the graph makes the method return `None`. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node where the path ends, given as an integer node ID or a string label, with the same rules as `source=`. If `target=` equals `source=`, the path is just that node. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store path position. If `None`, uses `shortest_path_order` as the attribute name. Only nodes on the path get this attribute set; positions are 0-based (`source=` is `0`), and all other nodes get a null value. Use a different name for each call to keep several paths side by side. Only used when `return_list=` is `False`. [return_list]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns list of node IDs in the path and leaves the node DataFrame untouched. If `False` (default), stores positions as node attributes under `attr_name=` and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[list[int], Graph, None]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_list=` is `True`: list of node IDs from source to target (inclusive), or `None` if no path exists. If `return_list=` is `False` it returns self for method chaining, or `None` if no path exists. Because of the latter, a chain such as `graph.shortest_path(...).plot()` fails when the target is unreachable. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `source=` or `target=` is an ID or label that does not exist in the graph. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} This directed graph has three routes from A to F: through B and C (three hops, total weight 4), through D (two hops, weight 6), and through E (two hops, weight 5). On an unweighted graph only hops count, so the method returns a two-hop route even though the weights are set: ::: {#88522c46 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec def build_routes(weighted): return ( ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=weighted) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", 2.0), ("C", "F", 1.0), ("A", "D", 3.0), ("D", "F", 3.0), ("A", "E", 2.0), ("E", "F", 3.0), ] ) ) graph = build_routes(weighted=False) path = graph.shortest_path("A", "F", return_list=True) [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in path] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['A', 'D', 'F'] ``` ::: ::: Building the same graph with `weighted=True` switches to Dijkstra's algorithm, and the longer but cheaper route through B and C (total weight 4) wins: ::: {#9dfd87c4 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} weighted_graph = build_routes(weighted=True) path = weighted_graph.shortest_path("A", "F", return_list=True) [weighted_graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in path] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['A', 'B', 'C', 'F'] ``` ::: ::: With `return_list=False` (the default), each node on the path gets its position as a node attribute, and every other node gets a null value. This is handy for coloring the route in a plot: ::: {#991e3295 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.shortest_path("A", "F") graph.get_node_df().select(["label", "shortest_path_order"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Chaining multiple calls stores each path under its own attribute name: ::: {#4c0ae628 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} grid = ( ec.Graph() .add_grid_2d(rows=4, cols=4) .shortest_path(1, 16, attr_name="corner_to_corner") .shortest_path(4, 13, attr_name="other_diagonal") ) grid.get_node_attrs("corner_to_corner") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` {3: 2, 1: 0, 12: 5, 4: 3, 2: 1, 16: 6, 8: 4} ``` ::: ::: Edges are followed only in their direction, so there is no path from F back to A. Both modes then return `None` (not the graph): ::: {#55f7d5aa .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} (graph.shortest_path("F", "A", return_list=True), graph.shortest_path("F", "A")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (None, None) ``` ::: :::
